content: World AIDS Day is observed annually on December 1 and is dedicated to increasing awareness about the AIDS pandemic, which is caused by the spread of HIV infection. This pandemic has affected millions of people worldwide, making it one of the most devastating epidemics in recorded history. In 2005 alone, AIDS claimed the lives of approximately 6 million people, including over half a million children. The concept of World AIDS Day was first introduced during the 1988 World Summit of Ministers of Health on Programs for AIDS Prevention. Since its inception, the day has been embraced by governments, international organizations, and charities across the globe. From its establishment until 2004, the UNAIDS organization led the World AIDS Day campaign, selecting annual themes in collaboration with other global health organizations. In 2005, the responsibility for the campaign was transferred to the World AIDS Campaign (WAC), which adopted the overarching theme Stop AIDS: Keep the Promise for World AIDS Day observances through 2010. Each year, specific sub-themes were chosen to complement this main theme. The Stop AIDS: Keep the Promise theme is not limited to World AIDS Day but is used year-round by the WAC to promote HIV/AIDS awareness in the context of other significant global events, such as the G8 Summit. The World AIDS Campaign also conducts localized campaigns worldwide, such as the Student Stop AIDS Campaign in the United Kingdom, which focuses on raising awareness about HIV infection among young people. On World AIDS Day, it is common to hold memorials to honor those who have died from HIV/AIDS. Government and health officials often participate in the observance by delivering speeches or hosting forums to discuss AIDS-related topics. Since 1995, the President of the United States has issued an official proclamation recognizing World AIDS Day, and governments of other nations have followed suit with similar announcements.
